about: What each instrument mode can do, read from that instrument's own documentation and cited. A mode key here is a mode key one of the ledgers uses, and query.test.mts ties the two together. A mode whose numbers are not stated by its documentation is left out, and the query reports it as capabilities not recorded rather than guessing. Coverage is a list of intervals in micrometres, one per documented window, filter or channel, never an enclosing minimum and maximum: a request that falls in a gap is refused. Wavelengths are micrometres, apertures metres, pixel scales arcsec per pixel; where a mode has several cameras the finest pixel scale is the one recorded, because the query uses it only as a floor that an observation cannot beat. A pixel scale is sampling, not resolution: what the optics can resolve is the diffraction limit of the aperture, or a point spread function the documentation states, and the two are reported separately. Spitzer's 0.85 m aperture is from its telescope handbook: https://irsa.ipac.caltech.edu/data/SPITZER/docs/spitzermission/missionoverview/spitzertelescopehandbook/6/.

modes.instrumentResolutionBasis: the mirror assembly's point spread function, under 0.5 arcsec full width at half maximum with the detector, on axis
modes.note: The guide states no bandpass, so the coverage here is where the front-illuminated detector's quantum efficiency is above 30 per cent, 0.7 to 11.0 keV, converted at 1.23984 nm per keV. The mirrors are grazing incidence, so the diffraction limit is meaningless and the two-pixel floor is what the query uses. Aperture is the largest mirror shell (https://cxc.harvard.edu/proposer/POG/html/chap1.html). The detector pixel is wider than the mirrors' point spread function, and CIAO can position events inside a pixel (https://cxc.harvard.edu/ciao/why/acissubpix.html), so the pixel is sampling, not a resolution limit.

modes.instrumentResolutionBasis: the mirror assembly's point spread function, under 0.5 arcsec full width at half maximum with the detector, on axis
modes.note: Coverage is where the back-illuminated detector's quantum efficiency is above 30 per cent, 0.4 to 10.0 keV, converted at 1.23984 nm per keV. See ACIS-I for the aperture and why only the pixel floor is used. The detector pixel is wider than the mirrors' point spread function, and CIAO can position events inside a pixel (https://cxc.harvard.edu/ciao/why/acissubpix.html), so the pixel is sampling, not a resolution limit.

The pixels are 0.028 by 0.025 arcsec; the finer side is recorded. The detector stopped working in 2007.
The pixels are 0.034 by 0.030 arcsec; the finer side is recorded.
Aperture from the HST primer (https://hst-docs.stsci.edu/hsp/the-hubble-space-telescope-primer-for-cycle-34/hst-primer-optical-performance-guiding-performance-and-observing-efficiency).
The handbook states the detector pixels in micrometres (6 by 24), not in arcsec, so no pixel scale is recorded and only the diffraction limit floors the sharpness here.

The blue Digicon's photocathode is "sensitive from 1150 Å to 5400 Å"; the range is reached in several grating settings and no single grating covers it. The FOS dispersed light onto a linear array of 512 diodes rather than onto sky pixels, and the handbook states aperture sizes on the sky (0.1 to 4.3 arcsec pre-COSTAR, about 0.86 of that after) rather than an arcsec per pixel, so no pixel scale is recorded and only the diffraction limit floors the sharpness here. FOS calibration is frozen and its pipeline is retired; the archive's own final product of one Europa observation is pinned and read (docs/hubble.md, archive-final products of retired instruments).

The red Digicon's photocathode "covered the wavelength range from 1620 Å to 8500 Å", in several grating settings. See FOS/BL for why no pixel scale is recorded. No observation of this detector is pinned here.

Detector 1 (Side 1) took the dispersers Cam-A imaged onto it, whose useful ranges table 34.1 gives as G140L 1100 to 1900 Å, G140M 1100 to 1900 and Echelle A 1100 to 1700; the two distinct intervals are recorded. The handbook also calls D1 best at "about 1050 to 1700 Å" and passing "only far-ultraviolet photons (1060 to 1800 Å)", which describe the detector's response rather than what a disperser reaches, so the table's figures are the ones used. The GHRS counted onto 512 diodes, 500 of them science diodes, and the handbook states aperture sizes on the sky (the large science aperture 1.74 arcsec square and the small one 0.22 arcsec square after COSTAR) rather than an arcsec per pixel, so no pixel scale is recorded. The mirror positions imaged the aperture for target acquisition, which is not a science product kind. GHRS calibration is frozen and its pipeline is retired; the archive's own final product of one Europa observation is pinned and read (docs/hubble.md, archive-final products of retired instruments).

Detector 2 (Side 2) took the dispersers Cam-B imaged onto it, whose useful ranges table 34.1 gives as G160M 1150 to 2300 Å, G200M 1600 to 2300, G270M 2000 to 3300 and Echelle B 1700 to 3200; each is recorded separately, because selecting a disperser selects its range. See HRS/1 for why no pixel scale is recorded. No observation of this detector is pinned here.

The four coronagraph filters, from their central wavelengths and bandwidths in table 2 of https://jwst-docs.stsci.edu/jwst-mid-infrared-instrument/miri-instrumentation/miri-filters-and-dispersers: F1065C 10.575 plus or minus 0.375, F1140C 11.30 plus or minus 0.40, F1550C 15.50 plus or minus 0.45 and F2300C 22.75 plus or minus 2.75. Selecting a filter selects its coronagraph, so the gaps between them are real.

Coverage is the union of the twelve sub-band ranges bands.mts already states, 4.90 to 27.90 micrometres. The pixel scale is the average detector pixel; cubes are built on a finer spaxel, which does not make the data sharper.
The documentation gives one range for both low-resolution modes.
Two documented windows, 1.8 to 2.2 and 2.8 to 5.0 micrometres. Between them the mode observes nothing, so a request there is refused rather than met.

The short-wave channel covers 0.6 to 2.3 micrometres at 0.031 arcsec per pixel and the long-wave channel 2.4 to 5.0 at 0.063; they are separate intervals and the finer pixel scale is recorded. Aperture from https://jwst-docs.stsci.edu/jwst-observatory-hardware/jwst-telescope.

The four masking filters, at their half-power wavelengths in table 1 of https://jwst-docs.stsci.edu/jwst-near-infrared-imager-and-slitless-spectrograph/niriss-instrumentation/niriss-filters: F277W, F380M, F430M and F480M. The mode's own table quotes 2.8 to 4.8 micrometres, which spans three gaps. The product is an interferogram read as an image.
Coverage is the union of the nine grating and filter ranges bands.mts already states, 0.60 to 5.30 micrometres; no single grating covers all of it.
Pixel scale from the instrument's landing table; the shutters are 0.20 by 0.46 arcsec.
Pixel scale from the instrument's landing table; the documentation gives no finer per-mode value.

Coverage spans the four filters, blue 0.420 to 0.520, green 0.500 to 0.600, red 0.600 to 0.800 and methane 0.880 to 0.900 micrometres. The catalogue states a T number, not an f number, so no aperture is recorded and the query floors this mode on pixels alone. The pixel scale is 672.7 microradians at the centre of the field from the instrument paper (https://www.missionjuno.swri.edu/pub/e/downloads/JunoCam_Junos_Outreach_Camera.pdf), converted here; the JunoCam ledger states 675.4 microradians, which is 139.3 arcsec.

modes.instrumentResolutionBasis: the best mean in-flight IRAC point-response-function FWHM, channel 1; other cryogenic channels are 1.72 to 1.98 arcsec
modes.note: Each interval is the handbook's effective wavelength plus or minus half its documented bandwidth. The best channel's measured FWHM is a conservative possibility bound; publication still needs the selected channel and achieved PRF.

modes.instrumentResolutionBasis: the best mean in-flight IRAC point-response-function FWHM, channel 1; other cryogenic channels are 1.72 to 1.98 arcsec
modes.note: The archive mode changes the pointing pattern, not the four IRAC channels; see IRAC Map for how the intervals and best-case resolution are used.

modes.instrumentResolutionBasis: the best mean in-flight IRAC point-response-function FWHM, channel 1; other cryogenic channels are 1.72 to 1.98 arcsec
modes.note: An engineering request still reads the four IRAC arrays; a selected observation must establish which channels contain science-quality data.

modes.instrumentResolutionBasis: the best warm-mission mean IRAC point-response-function FWHM, channel 1; channel 2 is 2.02 arcsec
modes.note: Only channels 1 and 2 operated after cryogen exhaustion. Intervals use the handbook effective wavelengths and bandwidths.
The interval is the union of the handbook's delivered SL, LL, SH and LH module ranges. A selected AOR must identify which module and orders it used.
Spectral mapping steps the IRS slits across the target; the capability interval is the union of module ranges and the selected AOR must identify its module.

The blue and red peak-up filters overlap from 18.5 to 18.7 micrometres. Pixel scale uses the finer detector axis documented at https://irsa.ipac.caltech.edu/data/SPITZER/docs/irs/irsinstrumenthandbook/8/.
An engineering request can use the IRS modules; a selected observation must establish whether its product is science quality and which module it used.

modes.instrumentResolutionBasis: the best MIPS point-spread-function FWHM, at 24 micrometres; the 70 and 160 micrometre FWHMs are 18 and 40 arcsec
modes.note: The intervals are the handbook's 50 per cent response cut-on and cut-off wavelengths. The best channel's PSF is only a possibility bound; a selected AOR must identify its band.

modes.instrumentResolutionBasis: the best MIPS point-spread-function FWHM, at 24 micrometres; the 70 and 160 micrometre FWHMs are 18 and 40 arcsec
modes.note: Scan mapping uses one or more MIPS imaging bands; exact bands remain an observation-level fact.
The handbook gives a nominal 55 to 95 micrometre spectrum at resolving power about 15 to 25.

modes.instrumentResolutionBasis: the best point-spread-function FWHM of the 70 and 160 micrometre arrays used for total-power measurements
modes.note: Total Power measures absolute brightness of highly extended emission with the 70 and 160 micrometre arrays; it is not an image product.

modes.instrumentResolutionBasis: the best MIPS point-spread-function FWHM, at 24 micrometres
modes.note: An engineering request can use a MIPS array; a selected observation must establish whether its product is science quality and which band it used.

Pixel scale is CONICA's finest camera, S13 at 13.22 mas (https://eso.org/sci/facilities/paranal/instruments/naco/inst/conica.html); the aperture is a VLT Unit Telescope (https://www.eso.org/sci/facilities/paranal/telescopes/ut.html).
Simultaneous differential imaging around the 1.6 micrometre methane feature. CONICA's table gives the SDI+ camera 17.25 mas and the imaging page 17.32 mas; the finer of the two is recorded.
The range spans the grisms, from S54_4_SJ at 0.91 to 1.40 to L54_1_SL at 2.60 to 4.20; no single grism covers all of it. The pixel scale is the S54 camera the grisms use.
